title: Trello vs Gigxomi for Video Editing Project Management
excerpt: A practical Trello vs Gigxomi comparison for video editing teams choosing between simple kanban boards and connected agency operations.
seoDescription: Trello vs Gigxomi for video editing agencies: compare simple kanban boards with connected client, team, delivery, and payout operations.
featuredImageAlt: Trello versus Gigxomi project management comparison
introduction: Trello makes work visible through boards, lists, and cards, with automation and Power-Ups extending the model. Gigxomi represents a video editing agency as connected customers, managers, editors, production stages, review, delivery, accounting, and payouts. Trello can be the better tool when a clear board is enough; Gigxomi becomes more relevant when a card no longer carries the business context safely.
verdict: Choose Trello for an approachable kanban workflow, small teams, simple content pipelines, and processes everyone can understand at a glance. Choose Gigxomi when multiple client channels, role-based handoffs, review, delivery, and financial state must remain linked. Trello's simplicity is a strength until the team fills cards with fields, links, and checklists that simulate a larger application.

featureMatrix.gigxomi: Editing-specific state and permission logic is built into operations

sections.heading: The strength of a board everyone understands
paragraphs: A Trello production board can be taught in minutes: Brief received, Ready to assign, Editing, Internal review, Client review, Approved, Delivered. Editors drag cards, managers scan bottlenecks, and checklists capture repeatable export steps. That transparency often beats a sophisticated system nobody updates.

Trello is especially effective for a stable team with one intake channel and modest volume. Power-Ups and automation can add calendars, files, or scheduled actions without destroying the simple mental model. The product should not be dismissed merely because it looks lightweight.
bullets: Card checklists for repeatable quality control
Automation and Power-Ups for selective extension

sections.heading: Signs your Trello system is becoming a database
paragraphs: Warning signs include dozens of custom fields, multiple client boards with inconsistent lists, long comment threads copied from WhatsApp, links to separate review and finance sheets, and private cards used to hide payout data. The board still looks simple, but the true operating system is distributed across attachments and human memory.

Gigxomi addresses the connected model directly. A manager should be able to understand who the customer is, who owns production, what stage the work reached, and which financial state follows delivery without decoding a card convention created by a former employee.

sections.heading: Run a scale test, not only a feature test
paragraphs: Duplicate your busiest week in a sandbox: simultaneous feedback, an absent editor, a rush project, a client changing scope, and a payout dispute. Watch how many cards must move, how many people need manual messages, and whether restricted information remains private. A tool that works for ten calm cards may fail at one hundred active deliverables.

Ask each role to find an answer without assistance: the editor's next priority, the manager's blocked reviews, the owner's at-risk client, and finance's approved payout. Record the time and confidence of each answer. This reveals operational clarity better than comparing marketing checklists.

sections.heading: Migration advice from Trello
paragraphs: Archive closed boards and export them for records. Move only active cards, preserving original card URLs in a migration note when their comment history remains relevant. Translate lists into deliberate production states and map members to their real agency roles instead of recreating every workspace permission.

Stop using cards as parallel records after cutover. If a leadership board must remain, create one summary card per client or portfolio, not one duplicate card per video. Keep Trello for simple editorial calendars or brainstorming if it continues to serve those jobs well.

sections.heading: Choose based on coordination risk
paragraphs: Trello fits small teams that communicate closely, have predictable review paths, and benefit from a shared visual board. It also fits a content calendar where each card is genuinely self-contained and financial operations live safely elsewhere.

Gigxomi fits agencies where delegation creates risk: several managers, a network of editors, client conversations across messaging channels, approvals that affect delivery, and payouts that cannot be inferred from a Done column. The more relationships a card must imitate, the stronger the case for a specialist system.

decisionChecklist: Can a new editor understand every list and label without oral training?
How many external links are required to explain one active card?
Does each client board use the same production states?
Can sensitive payout context be separated from general board access?
What happens when an editor is replaced mid-project?
Would Trello remain useful for a separate lightweight calendar after migration?
